$comment: Guides for every user-facing screen (T-11.1, T-11.3, REQ-148, REQ-150). JSON rather than markdown because two things read this file: the app, which renders it with no parser and no dependency, and tests/test_docs.py, which fails the build when a route has no guide or a screenshot has gone stale. A format only one of them could read would let the two drift.

guides.title: Ask
guides.blurb: Ask a question in your own words and get an answer with the page it came from.

sections.heading: What it does
body: Type a question the way you would ask a person — *when did I last get the brakes done?* — and Bindery finds the pages that could answer it and reads them.
Every claim in the answer is linked to the page it came from. Click **Sources** to see them beside the answer.

sections.heading: When it says it cannot find something
body: An answer with nothing to cite is thrown away rather than shown with a caveat. A caveat is read once; an answer is believed.
You still get the pages that mention what you asked about, which is what the search box would have given you — often that is enough to see the thing yourself.

callout.text: Ask needs an API key, set in Settings. Everything else — search, the viewer, the archive — works without one and without a network.

guides.title: Search
guides.blurb: Every page in the archive, by the words printed on it.

sections.heading: It searches pages, not files
body: A result is *page 47 of a 100-page scan*, not *a 100-page scan*. Clicking it opens that page with your words highlighted.
This is the whole point of the archive: the DD-214 inside a bundle of everything else is findable without anyone having split the bundle up.

sections.heading: Narrowing it down
body: The filters down the side narrow by library, by kind of document, and by known forms. Everything you pick is in the address bar, so a search is a link you can send or bookmark.

sections.heading: If a search finds nothing
body: Check whether the words were ever read correctly. Open the file and use **See the extracted text** — handwriting and faint carbon copies are where OCR struggles, and seeing the raw text tells you whether to re-scan or search for something else.

guides.title: Add files
guides.blurb: Drag documents in and watch them move through the pipeline.

sections.heading: What happens to a file
body: The original is stored byte-for-byte and **never modified**. Everything Bindery does happens alongside it.
Then it is read: every page is OCR'd and indexed, which is what makes it findable. If a scan holds several documents, it is split by page range — again without touching the original.

sections.heading: Watching it happen
body: The pipeline on this page shows each file moving from stage to stage. A file that fails stops somewhere visible and says why; nothing disappears quietly.
**Open the log** shows every line the application wrote about your files, which is usually enough to explain a failure without asking anyone.

sections.heading: What it accepts
body: PDFs, photographs and scans (JPEG, PNG, TIFF, HEIC), and office documents — Word, Excel, PowerPoint, OpenDocument, RTF, CSV, plain text and HTML. Office files are converted to PDF and then travel the ordinary path; the original is kept and an export still hands back the .xlsx.

guides.title: Files
guides.blurb: The folder tree, and every file the archive has ever been given.

sections.heading: Files and documents are different things
body: A **file** is what you gave Bindery. A **document** is a range of pages within one — a twelve-page scan holding three documents is one file and three documents.
This screen is the file view: what arrived, when, from where, and what state it reached.

sections.heading: When something looks wrong
body: **See the extracted text** shows exactly what OCR read, verbatim. A search finding nothing is ambiguous until you can see whether the word was ever read correctly.
If it was not, a rescan re-runs OCR with more aggressive settings — and re-runs everything downstream of it, so the corrected text ends up in search.

guides.title: Review
guides.blurb: The documents Bindery was not confident enough to file on its own — and where you correct the ones it got wrong.

sections.heading: Why something is here
body: Filing is decided on **structural facts**, not on how confident the model says it is: whether the document matched a known form, whether every tag it chose already existed, whether the date was quoted from a labelled field.
Model confidence is shown, because it is interesting, and is deliberately not part of the decision. It is not well calibrated, and a system that files on it files wrongly with conviction.

sections.heading: Correcting it, then accepting
body: **Correct** opens the fields inline. Fix the title, the date, who it is from, its type, and its tags — then **Accept**. Until now the only answers were "accept all of it" and "throw all of it away", so "this is right except the date" meant accepting something wrong or rejecting something mostly right.

**What you set is yours.** Re-running AI review will keep improving the fields you have not touched and will leave the ones you have. A field you set is marked *you set this*, so finding it unchanged after a review run reads as correct rather than broken.
Every correction is one undoable action. **Undo last change** walks back the whole edit — the fields, the tags you added, and the tags you removed — and hands the fields back to AI review.

Typing a name that does not exist yet offers to **create** it, as an explicit choice. Nothing is ever matched by resemblance: taxonomy is linked by identity, so two things with similar names stay two things until you merge them on Organise.

sections.heading: The why panel
body: Every AI-written field points at the page and sentence that justified it. If a date looks wrong, you can see where it came from in one click.
Anything you change is recorded and can be undone — including un-filing something.

guides.title: Archive
guides.blurb: Browse everything, grouped the way you want to look at it.

sections.heading: Grouping
body: By year, by who it is from, by kind of document, or by known form. The grouping is a view — nothing is moved, and a document belongs to exactly one library regardless of how you are looking at it.

guides.title: Photos
guides.blurb: Photos and videos, as pictures — with what the files already knew about themselves.

sections.heading: Why pictures get their own screen
body: A photograph carries no text, so OCR finds nothing on it and a list of filenames is a poor way to look for one. A grid is not.
**Nothing readable on these** finds the images OCR could not read. Bindery can look at those and describe them — that is what the button does, and it costs an API call each.

sections.heading: Videos
body: Videos have their own tab. They are never OCR'd or sent to the model — there is nothing to read and nothing to say — so instead the archive reads what the file knows: how long it is, when it was shot, on what, and where. That becomes the searchable text, so *the clip from the lake in 2023* is findable.
Formats a browser plays — .mp4, .mov, .m4v, .webm — play here and seek. Others (.avi, .mkv, .wmv) are stored and offered as a download.

sections.heading: From the file
body: A photograph's capture date, camera and location are read from its EXIF and shown beside it. The capture date fills the document date when nothing else has, marked **from the file** — a fact the file carried, not a guess, and still outranked by anything you set yourself.

guides.title: Vault
guides.blurb: A second lock, with its own passphrase, for the things you would rather not have on screen.

sections.heading: What it actually does
body: Moving a document into the vault encrypts the original and **deletes the plaintext copy**. What is left on disk is ciphertext with a random name — nothing about the file name says what it holds.

It also leaves search, Ask, the archive, the photo wall and every count. Not filtered out of them: a locked vault reports that it exists and nothing else, because a count of what is inside is already a statement about the contents.
This can be undone. **Take out** decrypts it back into the archive with its title and page text, and it becomes searchable again.

sections.heading: Documents, photos and videos
body: The vault splits into two tabs, because a photograph in a table row is as unhelpful here as it is anywhere else. **Photos** shows them as pictures; **Documents** lists everything else. If everything you have vaulted is a picture, the vault opens on Photos.
Once the vault is open, its contents are readable — pictures included. Clicking one opens it full size, with **Take out of the vault** beside it.

These are the full originals, decrypted for you as the page loads. There are no thumbnails on purpose: a thumbnail is a plaintext copy of the thing you are hiding, and generating them would put that copy back on disk. Nothing here is cached, so locking the vault makes it unreadable again immediately.
A format your browser cannot draw — usually HEIC outside Safari — shows as a placeholder rather than an empty square. **Open original** still hands you the file.

A **Videos** tab appears when the vault holds any. They play from inside the vault: the file is stored in independently encrypted pieces, so seeking to the middle of a long clip decrypts only the part you are watching — not the whole file into memory.

sections.heading: The passphrase and the PIN
body: The passphrase is the real key and **cannot be recovered**. It is not stored anywhere — only a copy of the vault key wrapped with it. Nothing in Bindery, in the database, or in any backup can open the vault without it. Write it down somewhere physical.
The PIN is the everyday way in. Five wrong entries switch it off — that destroys the PIN wrapper and nothing else. The passphrase still opens everything and you can set a new PIN straight afterwards.
The vault locks itself after fifteen minutes of not being used, and restarting the server locks it too. The key lives in memory and never touches disk.

sections.heading: Searching it
body: Search has an **Also search the vault** section, off unless you ask for it, because the ordinary search is the one that runs over somebody's shoulder. Turning it on asks for the PIN.

Vault search decrypts and scans in memory rather than using an index. An index would mean writing the text back to disk in plaintext, which is the thing the vault exists to prevent. The cost is that it is linear — it tells you how many pages it scanned and how long it took, and says so plainly once that starts being slow.

sections.heading: Backups
body: Vaulted documents are backed up and replicated offsite like everything else, as ciphertext. A restore brings them back still sealed; they open with the passphrase and with nothing else.
The restore drill checks them: it verifies every sealed object came back and matches the hash recorded when it was uploaded. It does not decrypt them, because it cannot.

guides.title: Organise
guides.blurb: Tidy the folders, types and tags the archive has accumulated.

sections.heading: Near-duplicates
body: Twenty years of letterheads spell one organisation four ways. The near-duplicate list finds the ones that *look* alike, which is the right tool for a typo.

sections.heading: The unify pass
body: Some duplicates do not look alike at all — `Unit Patch` and `Insignia` are the same kind of document and share no letters. **Look for duplicates** asks a model, sending only the list of names and never any document text.
Nothing merges until you press the button on a group, and every merge can be undone on its own.

callout.text: Read each group before applying it. A general kind and a special case of it are different things — Receipt and Veterinary Receipt should stay apart — and the pass is deliberately cautious but not infallible.

guides.title: Import
guides.blurb: Bring a folder in — the inbox in one click — and see exactly what happened to every file.

sections.heading: Three steps
body: **Where from.** *Scan the inbox* looks at the watched folder every other feature already knows about. Or type any folder the worker can see.

**What it found.** How many files, how many are already here, duplicates within the batch, what the formats are, and what AI review would cost — before anything is read in. OCR, search and videos cost nothing; the estimate is only the optional classification step.
**Go.** Import everything in slices, try a sample first, or pause. Each slice is committed, so stopping is always safe and resuming is one click.

sections.heading: Straight into the vault
body: Tick **Straight into the vault** and every file is encrypted and taken out of the archive the moment its processing finishes. The archive itself does the sealing, so your vault has to be open while the import runs.

If the vault locks part-way — it does after fifteen minutes idle — the remaining files wait and the screen says **finished and waiting**, not done. Unlock it and they seal within a few seconds. The distinction is deliberate: a file sitting in the ordinary archive when you meant it for the vault should never look like success.

sections.heading: What happened
body: Every previous import is listed with what it imported, what was already here, and what failed. Open one to see each file, with the reason it failed, and the worker's own log lines for those files — written at the time, not reconstructed later.
Everything imported here is flagged as backlog and kept out of your daily review queue. It is searchable immediately either way.

guides.title: Trust
guides.blurb: Backups, exports, integrity, and everything the system has done.

sections.heading: The export is the important one
body: It writes a folder tree plus a plain `index.html` that opens in any browser with Bindery switched off. No scripts, no external assets.
That is the promise: your documents are not hostage to this software continuing to exist.

sections.heading: Integrity
body: Every original is content-addressed, so a changed byte is detectable. The integrity check re-hashes them and reports anything that no longer matches — bit rot found before a backup copies it.

guides.title: Pipeline
guides.blurb: Where every file is, and what went wrong with the ones that stopped.

sections.heading: Nothing fails silently
body: A file that cannot be processed lands in a visible state with the actual error, not a summary of it. Some failures are permanent and say so — a dynamic XFA form genuinely cannot be read by anything but Adobe.
Anything that gave up can be sent round again once whatever blocked it is fixed.

guides.title: Your account
guides.blurb: Password, two-factor authentication, and how much space you are using.

sections.heading: Two-factor
body: Optional for ordinary accounts, required for administrators. Turning it on means a stolen password is not enough on its own.
You are shown ten recovery codes once. Write them down — each works once and they are how you get in if you lose your phone.

sections.heading: Changing your password
body: Every other signed-in device is signed out, which is usually the reason for changing it.
If you have forgotten it, there is no reset email — ask whoever runs the server for a one-time code.

guides.title: People
guides.blurb: Invitations, accounts and storage. Administrators only.

sections.heading: What an administrator can and cannot do
body: They can invite, suspend, set storage limits, clear a lockout and issue a one-time password reset code.

They **cannot read anyone else's documents**. There is no view-as, no override and no support path that involves looking — the permission boundary has no administrator branch, and a test asserts it on every route that returns anything.

callout.text: That is deliberate and it has a cost: diagnosing someone's problem means working from job states and error messages rather than from the document. The alternative is telling people you can read their medical records.

sections.heading: Inviting someone
body: There is no email service, so you get a link to send yourself — by text, or in person. It works once and expires in a fortnight.
A reset code works the same way: you read it out, and they choose their own new password. You never learn what it is.

guides.title: Settings
guides.blurb: The API key, the model, and how the archive behaves.

sections.heading: Working without a key
body: Ingest, OCR, search, the viewer and export all work with no API key and no network. Only classification and Ask defer.
Documents added before a key was configured are not lost or broken — they wait, and can be sent through review whenever you add one.

guides.title: Rules
guides.blurb: Deterministic filing you wrote, which overrules the model.

sections.heading: Rules run after classification
body: The model proposes; a rule decides. If you know every statement from one bank is a bank statement, say so once and stop correcting it.
A rule's effects are recorded as coming from *your rule*, not from the model, so the why panel can tell you which of the two is responsible for a field.

sections.heading: Dry run first
body: Every rule can be tested against the archive before it is switched on: it shows what would change, on which documents, without changing anything.
Worth doing. A rule is applied retroactively, so a wrong one is wrong across everything at once — recoverable, since it is all undoable, but tedious.

faq.question: Can the person running this server read my documents?
faq.answer: No. An administrator can see your account, how much space you are using, and whether a file failed to process. They cannot open a document, see a title, or read a page. This is enforced in the code — the permission boundary has no administrator branch — and a test sweeps every route that returns data to prove it stays that way.

faq.question: What happens to my original files?
faq.answer: They are stored exactly as you gave them and never modified. Everything Bindery produces — the searchable text, the page images, the split into separate documents — lives alongside the original, never in place of it.

faq.question: Does anything ever get deleted?
faq.answer: No, and nothing is designed to. Deleting is not automated anywhere: merges tombstone rather than remove, corrections are recorded rather than overwritten, and there is no retention policy quietly tidying up behind you.

faq.question: I forgot my password.
faq.answer: There is no reset email, because there is no email service. Ask whoever runs the server for a one-time code; they generate it and read it to you, and you choose your own new password. They never learn what it is. Enter it on the sign-in page under **I have a reset code**. Codes last a day and each works once.

faq.question: Why is a document waiting for review instead of being filed?
faq.answer: Because the evidence for filing it was thin. Bindery files on structural facts — a matched known form, tags that all already existed, a date quoted from a labelled field — and not on how confident the model claims to be. Something with none of those waits for you rather than guessing.

faq.question: My search found nothing. Is the document missing?
faq.answer: Possibly not. Open the file and choose to see the extracted text: that shows exactly what OCR read. Handwriting and faint carbon copies are where it struggles, and seeing the raw text tells you whether to re-scan, or just to search for a different word.

faq.question: How much space do I have?
faq.answer: Your account page shows what you have used and your limit, if one was set. Uploads are refused before the file is stored once you are at the limit, and the message says the numbers. Ask for more if you need it.

faq.question: Can I get my documents out?
faq.answer: Yes, and this is worth testing rather than trusting. Trust → Export writes a folder tree plus a plain index.html that opens in any browser with Bindery switched off. Bundled scans stay as one file with the page ranges named, because splitting them would modify an original.

faq.question: Does anything I do here go to Anthropic?
faq.answer: Only classification and Ask, and only when an API key is configured. Those send the text of the pages being classified or consulted. Search, OCR, the viewer, the archive and export never leave the machine. The folder-tidying pass sends only the list of folder names, never any document text.
